analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals buy lower-priced prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to let Americans import prescription drugs from Canada died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA, within 180 days, to set up rules letting individuals import a 90-day personal supply of prescription drugs from Canadian pharmacies the FDA certifies as safe. The drugs would have to match FDA-approved versions in active ingredient, dose, and form, and controlled substances, biologics, and certain other drug types would be excluded. It was referred to the Senate Health Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially people on fixed incomes taking long-term medications that cost far less in Canada. A Congressional condition of the program is that only FDA-certified, long-established Canadian pharmacies could participate, and only for drugs identical to FDA-approved ones.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to issue regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to import a 90-day personal supply of qualifying prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
Limits imports to drugs with the same active ingredients, dosage form, route of administration, and strength as FDA-approved drugs, purchased with a valid U.S. prescription.

Restricts the program to certified Canadian pharmacies in operation at least five years, subject to quality-assurance and product-testing requirements, with a published FDA list so consumers know which sellers are approved.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose Canadian price controls make the same drugs far cheaper there; the bill lets Americans buy at those lower prices rather than U.S. list prices. U.S. pharmacies that dispense at higher domestic prices could also lose some sales.

drawbacks.text: Excludes major spending categories: the bill bars biological products, biotechnology-derived drugs such as monoclonal antibodies, refrigerated drugs, and intravenously injected drugs, so many of the most expensive treatments would not qualify.

Covers only personal importation in 90-day supplies, not bulk importation, so it would not change prices system-wide for insurers, employers, or people who need larger or ongoing supplies through regular channels.

Critics have long argued that personal importation carries safety and supply risks for the Canadian system, though the bill responds with certification, testing, and pharmacy-qualification requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For individuals who could use it, the benefit is direct and immediate: the same FDA-approved drug at Canadian prices, from pharmacies subject to FDA certification and testing. The design is deliberately narrow — no biologics, no bulk importation, 90-day supplies only — which limits both the savings and the risk, but also limits the impact on overall U.S. drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and received no further action of any kind before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 4, 2021, with 12 cosponsors from both parties, including Republican Senators Chuck Grassley and Susan Collins.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers avoided a legal channel that would have let Americans buy their products at Canadian prices, and the Senate committee process that took no action on the bill preserved that outcome.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require the FDA to allow personal drug importation from Canada.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from a senior Republican.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry
against.what_they_did: Has long campaigned against importation proposals as safety risks; the industry's opposition is the standing backdrop to why such bills rarely advance.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: 9 of 48 Democrats, 2 of 50 Republicans, and 1 of 2 Independents signed on, but no vote ever occurred so no party split was ever tested.

industries.note: Canadian price controls make identical drugs far cheaper there; the bill would have let Americans buy at those prices instead of U.S. list prices, cutting into manufacturer revenue on drugs sold to U.S. individuals. It died without a vote, so nothing changed.

The bill would have created an FDA-certified channel for them to serve U.S. customers legally, with a published list of approved pharmacies. Their gain comes from the same lower prices consumers would pay.
Some prescription volume could shift to Canadian sellers at lower prices, though the 90-day, non-biologic limits keep most routine fills in the U.S. system.
